title: The Internal Consistency of Scripture

keyTerms.t: A difference is not a contradiction
keyTerms.d: The law of non-contradiction states that the same proposition cannot be both true and false in the same sense at the same time. Two accounts contradict only if they cannot both be true — not merely if they differ, emphasize different things, or one mentions what the other omits.

The Bible is dozens of documents written by perhaps forty authors over roughly fifteen centuries, in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek, spanning law, chronicle, poetry, prophecy, proverb, letter, apocalypse, and ancient biography. Genre governs what counts as accuracy: a parable is not falsified by being fictional.

Selection is not denial; difference is not discrepancy; accuracy is not precision; paraphrase is not misquotation; thematic ordering is not error. A misconstrued referent or a frank mystery is not the same thing as a demonstrated contradiction. The toolkit is for disciplined humility, not a skeleton key that opens every lock.

The rule, in A. T. Robertson’s words: “even a possible explanation is sufficient to meet the objector.” A possible reconciliation is enough to defeat the charge of a formal contradiction — one need not prove which harmonization is the correct one, only that the two statements can both be true. The humility runs the other way too: it licenses no pretense that every hard case has been tidily solved.

Bart Ehrman’s method: stop reading the Gospels “vertically,” each blended into a single harmonized story, and set parallel accounts side by side, noticing where they conflict. The differences his cases point to are really there in the text.

The Gospels belong to the genre of Greco-Roman biography. Michael Licona catalogued how Plutarch, telling the same episode more than once, compresses time, transfers a saying, displaces events, simplifies participants, and paraphrases — accepted devices taught in the rhetorical handbooks. The thesis is contested, by skeptics and by some inerrantist scholars alike.

Accounts that differ on incidentals but converge on a common core show the pattern of substantially independent witnesses — the pattern courts treat as a mark of authenticity rather than collusion. Independent testimony to a real event almost never lines up perfectly; perfect alignment would smell of collusion.

Demonstrating consistency removes a defeater; it does not, by itself, prove the contents true — an internally consistent novel is still a novel. Clearing away the charge of contradiction only earns the texts a fair hearing; it does not win the case.

derive.q: One account mentions one angel at the tomb, another mentions two — for this to be a contradiction, the two reports must…?
derive.ans: be unable both to be true
derive.why: Two accounts contradict only if they cannot both be true — not merely if they differ, emphasize different things, or one mentions what the other omits. “There was an angel at the tomb” and “there were two angels at the tomb” are not formal contradictories: a report of one does not deny a second unless it says “only one.”

derive.q: A critic demands you prove which harmonization actually happened — to defeat a charge of formal contradiction you need…?
derive.ans: only a possible reconciliation, not proof of which
derive.why: “Even a possible explanation is sufficient to meet the objector”: one need not prove which harmonization is the correct one, only that the two statements can both be true. But the humility runs the other way as well — none of this licenses the pretense that every hard case has been tidily solved.

derive.q: Plutarch, one respected ancient author, narrates the same event two ways — compressing, transferring, paraphrasing — so where the Gospels do the same, those features are…?
derive.ans: fingerprints of the genre, not of falsehood
derive.why: These were accepted compositional devices, taught in the rhetorical handbooks, not errors by the standards of the day. But the thesis is contested, and not only by skeptics: it explains why the differences exist and shows they were not regarded as falsehoods; it does not turn every hard case into a smooth one. It lowers the temperature; it does not end the debate.

derive.q: John may mean “the Friday of Passover week,” or may have shaped his chronology theologically — on either reading, the central claim…?
derive.ans: Jesus crucified under Pilate at Passover — stands untouched
derive.why: This is a case where the data underdetermine the answer. The most defensible position is not “there is obviously no difference” but “there is a real difference, there are serious explanations of it, and on either reading the central claim — that Jesus was crucified under Pilate at Passover — stands untouched.”

derive.q: Four accounts of the same event that matched word for word would suggest…?
derive.why: Independent testimony to a real event almost never lines up perfectly — and perfect alignment, far from reassuring us, would smell of collusion. Accounts that diverge on the surface and converge on the core are what truthful, substantially independent testimony looks like.

derive.q: Grant that the Bible is substantially consistent — does that prove its contents true?
derive.ans: no — it removes a defeater; truth is argued separately
derive.why: An internally coherent account can still be mistaken, and clearing away the charge of contradiction only earns the texts a fair hearing. Whether what the authors wrote is reliable turns on other arguments, including whether the text has been faithfully preserved; whether it is true — up to and including Easter morning — is argued on its own ground, in the historical case for the resurrection.

honestState.p1: On the wider claim — that Scripture’s many books cohere into one developing storyline — many scholars across confessions recognize a real narrative unity, however they explain it. On the narrower question of Gospel discrepancies, the field is genuinely divided, and the division is honest. Critics like Bart Ehrman hold that some differences are true contradictions that no harmonization repairs without special pleading. Defenders like Craig Blomberg and Michael Licona hold that, read in their ancient context, the differences are overwhelmingly the expected variation of independent and genre-bound testimony. Many scholars who affirm the Gospels’ substantial reliability accept that the Evangelists used ancient compositional conventions while denying that this amounts to error; others who hold a stricter view of inerrancy have criticized that position, which shows the debate is live inside the church as well as across its borders. That intra-Christian debate is reported here without adjudicating it.
honestState.fairness: Honest defenders concede that Ehrman is right that crude harmonization can distort the text, and right that the Evangelists were authors with theological aims, not stenographers. They concede that some cases are genuinely hard: the Judas harmonization is an inference we supply, not something either text states; the day of the crucifixion is a case where the data underdetermine the answer; and the usual harmonizations of the Galilee and Jerusalem appearances are plausible but not airtight. But conceding a real difference is not conceding a contradiction: a possible reconciliation is enough to defeat the charge of a formal contradiction, and on either reading of the hardest case the central claim — that Jesus was crucified under Pilate at Passover — stands untouched.
honestState.verdict: Is the Bible internally consistent? With the difference/contradiction distinction in hand, the genre of each text respected, and the conventions of ancient writing taken seriously, the answer is: substantially yes, with a handful of genuinely hard cases that remain debated and that honesty forbids us to pretend away. The honest verdict is not that every difference dissolves, but that the residue of genuinely hard cases is small, peripheral, and powerless to overturn the central narrative the accounts all share. Many scholars across confessions recognize a real narrative unity, however they explain it; this page offers a single guiding Author as the best explanation — a pointer, not a proof. And consistency removes a defeater; it does not, by itself, prove the contents true. Whether what the authors wrote is reliable turns on other arguments, including whether the text has been faithfully preserved; whether it is true — up to and including Easter morning — is argued on its own ground, in the historical case for the resurrection.

order: Writings by dozens of authors over many centuries that present one coherent, developing message are best explained by a guiding mind behind them.

Scripture, written by perhaps forty authors over roughly fifteen centuries, displays this unity — partly by inheritance, but also in forward-leaning patterns its earliest authors could not have engineered.
Therefore the unity of Scripture is best explained by a single guiding Author behind its many human writers — a pointer, not a proof.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and what kind of argument it is.
cards.a: If writings by dozens of authors over many centuries present a single, coherent and developing message, that unity is best explained by a guiding mind behind it. It is an inference to the best explanation — a pointer, not a proof.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and which part of the unity inheritance alone does not explain.
cards.a: Scripture, written by perhaps forty authors over roughly fifteen centuries, displays this unity. Later authors did write within the earlier books, and that inheritance explains some of it; what is hardest to explain on inheritance alone is the forward-leaning pattern the earliest authors could not have engineered.

cards.q: What does consistency reach — and not reach?
cards.a: Demonstrating consistency removes a defeater and earns the texts a fair hearing; it does not, by itself, prove the contents true — an internally consistent novel is still a novel. Whether they are true, up to and including Easter morning, is argued on its own ground, in the historical case for the resurrection.

cards.q: When do two accounts actually contradict?
cards.a: Only if they cannot both be true — not merely if they differ, emphasize different things, or one mentions what the other omits. A report of one angel does not deny a second unless it says “only one.”

cards.q: Give three cautionary principles for weighing an alleged contradiction — and their purpose.
cards.a: Selection is not denial; difference is not discrepancy; accuracy is not precision (also: paraphrase is not misquotation; thematic ordering is not error). Their purpose is disciplined humility, not a skeleton key that opens every lock.

cards.q: How much must a defender show to defeat a charge of formal contradiction — and what is the limit?
cards.a: Only that the two statements can both be true — a possible reconciliation, not proof of which harmonization is correct. The humility runs both ways: not having an answer is not the same as there being no answer, but nothing licenses the pretense that every hard case has been tidily solved.

cards.q: What does comparing Plutarch’s retellings with the Gospels show — and not show?
cards.a: One respected ancient author, narrating the same event two ways, compresses, transfers, displaces, simplifies and paraphrases as the Gospels do — so these are fingerprints of the genre, not of falsehood. But the thesis is contested, and not only by skeptics: it lowers the temperature; it does not end the debate.

cards.q: Why would four perfectly matching accounts be a worse sign, not a better one?
cards.a: Independent testimony to a real event almost never lines up perfectly; perfect alignment would smell of collusion. Accounts that differ on incidentals but converge on a core show the pattern of substantially independent witnesses.

cards.q: What core do the resurrection accounts converge on — and what is the caveat about Mark?
cards.a: Jesus was buried, the tomb was found empty on the first day of the week, women were the first witnesses, and the risen Jesus appeared. Mark, the earliest Gospel, points forward to appearances in Galilee (Mark 16:7) even though its undisputed text breaks off at the empty tomb.

cards.q: Matthew and Acts on Judas’s death — what does the standard harmonization achieve, and what does it not?
cards.a: Judas hanged himself, the body later fell and burst, and the field was bought with his returned money — a sequence possible and not contrived. It removes the charge of strict contradiction; but it is an inference we supply, not something either text states.

cards.q: Mark and John on the day of the crucifixion — what is the most defensible position?
cards.a: Not “there is obviously no difference” but “there is a real difference, there are serious explanations of it, and on either reading the central claim — that Jesus was crucified under Pilate at Passover — stands untouched.” The data underdetermine the answer.

cards.q: Does the debate over Gospel differences settle the inerrancy question?
cards.a: No. Many who affirm the Gospels’ reliability accept that the Evangelists used ancient compositional conventions while denying this amounts to error; others who hold a stricter view of inerrancy have criticized that position. The debate is live inside the church, and this argument reports it without adjudicating it.

obj.q: Read the Gospels horizontally, as Bart Ehrman urges, and the discrepancies reach into the narratives themselves. In Mark the Last Supper is a Passover meal (Mark 14:12), so Jesus dies on the day of Passover; in John he dies on “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (John 19:14), as the lambs are being slaughtered — a full day earlier. They cannot both be right.
obj.model: Grant what is true in it: the difference is really there in the text, and it is the most discussed case of all. But the strongest harmonizations are substantive, not hand-waving: “day of Preparation” (paraskeuē) is the ordinary word for Friday, the day of preparation for the Sabbath, so John may simply mean “the Friday of Passover week”; and there is solid evidence that different Jewish groups followed different calendars, so a Passover celebrated on different days is historically possible. Yet many scholars — including some who fully affirm the Gospels’ reliability, Licona among them — judge that John has, for profound theological reasons, presented Jesus as the true Passover Lamb dying as the lambs were slain, and that this shapes his chronology. This is a case where the data underdetermine the answer. The most defensible position is not “there is obviously no difference” but “there is a real difference, there are serious explanations of it, and on either reading the central claim — that Jesus was crucified under Pilate at Passover — stands untouched.” So the objection names a genuinely hard case; like the rest of that small residue, it is powerless to overturn the central narrative the accounts share.

obj.q: Matthew says Judas threw the silver into the temple and “went and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5); Acts says he “fell headlong” in a field he had bought, “and all his bowels gushed out” (Acts 1:18). The two even disagree on who bought the field. A hanged man does not fall and burst.
obj.model: The standard harmonization is possible and not contrived: Judas hanged himself (Matthew), the body later fell and burst (Acts), and the “purchase” in Acts is loosely attributed to Judas because the field was bought with his returned money. The objection that a hanged body cannot later fall underestimates decomposition and time. Concede the rest honestly: the accounts were plainly written for different purposes and never meant to be read against each other, and the harmonization, while reasonable, is an inference we supply, not something either text states. It removes the charge of strict contradiction; it does not pretend the two passages are saying the same thing. So the charge of strict contradiction does not hold — and the case stays one we concede as hard rather than hammering flat.

obj.q: Harmonizers cheat. To reconcile the accounts you must invent a fifth Gospel that none of the four actually wrote, splicing details into a composite story that flattens each author’s distinct theological voice. The differences are not accidental noise; each Evangelist shaped the tradition to make his own point.
obj.model: Concede the strongest point first: crude harmonization can distort the text, and the Evangelists were authors with theological aims, not stenographers. The question is whether that makes their differences contradictions. To defeat a charge of formal contradiction one need not prove which harmonization is the correct one, only that the two statements can both be true — “even a possible explanation is sufficient to meet the objector.” Even the fullest harmonization of Easter morning, John Wenham’s, is necessarily conjectural, and establishes only that the divergence is no demonstrable contradiction, not the actual order events took. And shaping is not falsifying: Licona’s Plutarch comparison shows a single respected ancient author narrating the same event two ways, doing precisely what the Gospels do — the fingerprints of the genre, not of falsehood — though that thesis is itself contested, and lowers the temperature rather than ending the debate. So the charge does not hold against the claim made here: crude harmonization can flatten the voices, but showing that two accounts can both be true is not writing a fifth Gospel.

obj.q: You have conceded the game. Once you admit John shaped his chronology theologically and Judas’s death needs an unstated splice, the Gospels are reshaping events to make points, and calling that “genre” is a sophisticated relabeling: the honest word for an author who moves an event for effect is that he got it wrong. The accounts cannot even agree on the appearances — Matthew and Mark point the disciples to Galilee, while Luke keeps the appearances in and around Jerusalem.
obj.model: Accuracy is genre-relative. A documentary and a docudrama can portray the same event with different levels of literal precision, and we do not call the docudrama a pack of lies; we judge it by its own conventions. When, in Licona’s comparison, a single respected ancient author narrates the same event two ways, he does what the Gospels do — a thesis contested within the church as well as outside it; and Craig Keener, setting Suetonius’s and Tacitus’s accounts of the emperor Otho side by side, finds them diverging in order, emphasis and detail as freely as any two Gospels while converging enough to show both drew on earlier sources. Ehrman is right that the Evangelists are authors with aims; he is wrong to assume that a first-century author exercising the ordinary liberties of his craft is thereby “getting it wrong” by his own culture’s lights. The location of the appearances is the genuinely harder divergence, and the usual harmonizations are plausible but not airtight — yet it is narrower than it first looks: Luke’s own sequel presupposes appearances over “forty days” (Acts 1:3), Matthew and Mark direct the disciples to Galilee without ever denying appearances in Jerusalem, and John, writing independently, reports both. So the objection does not hold: not every difference dissolves, but the residue of genuinely hard cases is small, peripheral, and powerless to overturn the central narrative they all share.

unseen.q: Matthew traces Jesus’ line through David’s son Solomon and says Joseph’s father was Jacob; Luke traces it through Nathan and says Joseph’s father was Heli. Joseph cannot have two fathers. That is not a difference of emphasis — it is a flat contradiction.
unseen.model: The two genealogies are best read as a real difference with more than one reasonable explanation rather than a flat contradiction. The oldest solution, going back to the African church father Julius Africanus in the third century, appeals to levirate marriage, by which Joseph could be the legal son of one man and the biological son of another. A common modern proposal holds that Matthew gives Joseph’s line while Luke gives Mary’s. Honesty requires admitting that neither solution is certain, and that the texts do not tell us which (if either) is right — the harmonization is plausible but not provable. What can be said is that the two genealogies are not formal contradictories: a line traced legally and a line traced biologically can both be true of the same man. And a possible reconciliation is enough to defeat the charge of a formal contradiction. So the charge of a flat contradiction does not hold — though which explanation is right, the texts leave open.
